title: Metzora: the priest goes out (Leviticus 14:3)
hookLine: the priest goes outside the camp to the person, not the other way round

lines: THE WAITING ROOM AND THE CLIPBOARD.
cards: Day four hundred. In our world, healing usually runs one way. You make the appointment, find the parking, sit in the waiting room with a clipboard.
The sick person does the traveling, because that's where the expert is. The next portion, Metzora, opens with a person who has been living outside the camp with tzara'at. Maybe the mark has faded.
Maybe they're ready to come home. But they aren't allowed back in to ask. So the Torah turns the usual direction around.

teach.b: Metzora means the afflicted one, the person with tzara'at, and the whole portion is about their way back.
The verse, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "the priest shall go forth out of the camp". The person can't come to the center, so the center comes to them.
The priest, whose place is at the sanctuary, walks past the last tent to where the outsider lives, and looks. His job here isn't only to judge. It's to be the bridge back.
Some commentators notice that the person outside has no way to start their own return.
Someone from inside has to make the first move. It feeds a whole tradition.
Jewish law calls visiting the sick bikur cholim, and treats it as a duty, not a favor.
The Talmud teaches that the Torah's command to walk after God means copying God's ways: as God visited Abraham while he was recovering, so you visit the sick.
Another passage says a visitor takes away one sixtieth of the sick person's suffering. Not a cure.
A sliver, but a real one. Some communities have a bikur cholim committee, people who go to hospitals and homes so no one is left alone.
Not the outsider going to the center, but the center going out: the same shape as a casserole on a doorstep, or a hospital visit on a weeknight.

how: Visiting the sick, bikur cholim, is counted among the acts of kindness in Jewish law, and some synagogues and communities run bikur cholim groups that visit hospitals, homes and care facilities.

games.q: someone outside the camp may be healed, but they can't come in to be seen. what does the Torah have happen?
o: they wait until someone hears about it.
the priest goes out of the camp to them.
they send word through a friend.
games.why: the priest goes forth out of the camp. the center comes to the outsider, not the other way round.

practice: Think of someone who can't easily get to you right now: sick, elderly, housebound, a new parent, without a car, or just stuck.
Picture where they are and what their day looks like from there, and let a visit, a call or a small delivery take shape in your mind. If you pray, hold them in your prayers.

wordCard.voice: Metzora. The afflicted one: the portion that opens with the priest going out of the camp to them, not waiting for them to come in.
